title: “RENDER UNTO CAESAR” — JESUS WAS SAYING MORE THAN “PAY YOUR TAXES”
paragraphs:
“RENDER UNTO CAESAR” — JESUS WAS SAYING MORE THAN “PAY YOUR TAXES”
We remember the coin. We remember Caesar. But we may have missed the devastating question hidden inside Jesus’ answer: If Caesar’s image tells you what belongs to Caesar… whose image is on you?
There is a moment in the Gospel of Matthew that most Christians have heard so many times that we can almost finish Jesus’ sentence before He says it.
“Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.”

Those applications are not meaningless. Scripture elsewhere does address governing authorities and taxes. Paul explicitly tells believers to pay what is owed, including taxes and revenue, in Romans 13:6–7.
But if we reduce Matthew 22 to a lesson about paying taxes, we may walk away staring at Caesar’s coin while completely missing the far more terrifying question Jesus placed before the human soul.
Because Jesus did not merely ask them about money.
He asked them about an image.
And once you see what happens in that conversation, His words become difficult to forget.

Matthew tells us they deliberately plotted to “entangle him in his talk.” Then they sent their disciples together with the Herodians—a striking combination because these groups did not naturally represent the same interests.
“Teacher, we know that thou art true…”
Sometimes the most dangerous words spoken to you are the ones designed to make you comfortable enough to destroy yourself.
“Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?”
The tax in view was the imperial poll tax imposed upon subject peoples.
Say yes, and Jesus could appear to side with the occupying imperial system in the eyes of people who resented Roman domination.
Say no, and His opponents could potentially portray Him as opposing Roman authority.
They were trying to trap the One who knew what was inside the trapper.
Then He said something almost painfully simple.
And suddenly the entire conversation changed.
Jesus did not produce the coin.
That detail deserves to sit with us for a moment.
The people attempting to trap Jesus over the legitimacy of Caesar’s tax were carrying Caesar’s currency.
The denarius circulated within Rome’s economic world, and the coin involved would have borne the image of the emperor; the NET Bible’s notes identify the figure as Tiberius Caesar.
In the Greek text, the crucial word is:
What is stamped on this thing?
“Ἀπόδοτε οὖν τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῷ Θεῷ.”
“Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
It carries the sense of giving back, paying, or rendering what is due. That is why translations legitimately render the statement as “render,” “give back,” or “pay.”
Caesar’s image was stamped on the coin.
Give Caesar what belongs to Caesar.
But Jesus did not stop there.
“…and to God the things that are God’s.”
And now the question becomes infinitely larger.
Jesus had just directed their attention to an image.
But where else had Israel heard language about an “image”?
They had heard it at the beginning of everything.
“Let us make man in our image, after our likeness…”
Human beings were created in the image of God.

The Greek Septuagint—the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament—uses the same key noun, εἰκών, in Genesis 1:26 for “image.” The lexical connection between Matthew’s εἰκών and Genesis is real; the NET Bible notes specifically identify this Genesis-image resonance as an important way of understanding Jesus’ contrast.
And suddenly the coin in Jesus’ hand becomes a mirror.
Caesar stamped his image on silver.
God stamped His image upon humanity.
Caesar may have a claim upon the coin.
God has a claim upon you.
And this is where the passage stops being an argument from two thousand years ago and begins looking directly at us.
Because we are very good at giving God things.
A little money when we have enough.
A promise after we have sinned again.
A tear when life finally becomes unbearable.
Maybe that is why this passage can be so uncomfortable.
The question is no longer merely, “Did you pay what you owe?”
Have you given God what bears His image?
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that question hurts.
At least you believe you do.
But there is a locked room inside your life where you have quietly hung a sign that says:
You can have my church attendance.
You can have my public Christianity.
Just don’t touch the bitterness I have protected for ten years.
Just don’t ask me to forgive them.
As long as Your future looks like mine.
And somehow we have learned how to sing “I surrender all” while negotiating the definition of “all.”
He sees what nobody else sees.
He knows where your excuses begin.
And He knows what belongs to God.
But if we stop there, we have not yet reached the Gospel.
Because the One demanding that we give ourselves to God is the same One who was preparing to give Himself for sinners.
Matthew 22 happens during the final stretch toward the cross.
Soon the hands holding that coin would be pierced.
The Teacher they attempted to trap would be arrested.
The innocent One would be treated like the guilty.
The sinless Christ would be mocked, beaten, crucified and killed.
And above His head another inscription would appear.
“This is Jesus the King of the Jews.”
The world put a title over the dying Christ.
But heaven knew what was really happening beneath it.
The Son of God was giving Himself for sinners.
Christianity is not the story of good people successfully rendering enough goodness to God until God accepts them.
It is the story of sinners who could never repay their debt being rescued by a Savior who paid what they could not pay.
Jesus Christ “gave himself for our sins” according to Galatians 1:4.
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” in 1 Peter 3:18.
Paul says that in Christ “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” in Ephesians 1:7.
Not God pretending your sin did not matter.
God dealing with sin at the cross.
Not Jesus helping decent people become slightly better.
Jesus rescuing sinners who could not rescue themselves.
Maybe your life does not look like something God would want right now.
Maybe you have spent years giving yourself away to things that never loved you back.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A carefully maintained Christian reputation covering a starving soul.
Grace does not tell you the chains are imaginary.
Grace does not rename darkness so you can remain comfortable inside it.
Grace calls you into the light.
Grace does not say, “Continue exactly as you are.”
Repentance is not God stealing your life.
It is returning to the One your life belonged to from the beginning.
The coin belonged to Caesar because Caesar’s image was stamped upon it.
You belong to God because you bear the image of your Creator.
And through the Gospel something even more astonishing happens: those who belong to Christ are being renewed according to the image of the One who created them, as Colossians 3:10 teaches.
It has not made God surrender His redemptive purpose.
The Gospel is Christ taking people whose stories look ruined and making them new.
Grace stopped him on the road.
The thief beside Jesus reached the final hours of a wasted life.
Grace met him on a cross.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated history.
The prodigal smelled like the country he had wasted himself in.
Again and again Scripture tells the same impossible story.
A past that appears to have written the final chapter…
And maybe tonight the coin is in your hand.
Maybe Jesus is asking you the question you have spent months avoiding.
Not the opinion of the people who abandoned you.
Not the label somebody placed on you during the worst season of your life.
You were made in the image of God.
And if you are in Christ, your deepest identity is not the scandal behind you but the Savior who redeemed you.
So yes—render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.
We should not erase the straightforward civic dimension of His answer.
But please do not walk away after handing Caesar his coin.
“…and unto God the things that are God’s.”
Because the coin may leave your hand.
But God asks for the hand holding it.
The person who promised God last time would be the last time.
The person wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want someone who knew better and sinned anyway.
Bring that person to the cross.
Receive the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
Then get up and follow Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
If you need prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”

If Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another exhausted believer realizes there is still hope.
There may come a night when you need these words again.
If these resources are feeding you spiritually, stay close.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer quietly fighting an addiction.
Invite the person angry with God.
Invite the person who thinks Jesus could never want them again.
He is the center of it.
We cannot resurrect a dead heart.
So share this because somebody needs Christ, not because an algorithm needs another post.
Follow because your soul needs more than endless noise.
And support Gospel work freely and prayerfully wherever God leads you, because the message is too precious to become merely another piece of content we consume and forget.
Rulers become names in history books.
But the image God placed upon humanity points to something no empire can own.
And the Savior who held that denarius eventually stretched those same hands upon a cross to redeem sinners.
So the next time you hear, “Render unto Caesar,” remember the question behind the coin.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be failing to give Caesar his coin.
It would be spending your entire life giving everything else pieces of yourself…
and never surrendering yourself to the God whose image you carried all along.
The coin bore Caesar’s face—but your life bears the fingerprints of God, and Jesus did not go to the cross merely to improve your story; He came to redeem it.
